hypothesis: An adversary who compromised Windows hosts in this network stole credentials from them (MITRE ATT&CK tactic: Credential Access).

frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network is stealing credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: Observable evidence such as LSASS process memory access (e.g., via Mimikatz or procdump), suspicious access to SAM/SECURITY registry hives, use of Windows Credential Manager APIs, or anomalous authentication events indicating credential theft.
frame.what_would_refute: Absence of any credential dumping tool execution, no unauthorized access to LSASS or registry hives, and no anomalous credential-related events on the compromised Windows hosts.

verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: pbeesly ran a PowerShell credential-collection toolkit (Get-PrivateKeys, Get-Keystrokes, Invoke-ScreenCapture, Invoke-Exfil) on scranton, and PowerShell processes opened LSASS with full access.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: powershell.exe (scranton) and wsmprovhost.exe (nashua) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF under user pbeesly, confirmed by Security 4656 AccessMask 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: SAM registry writes were performed by lsass.exe itself; no reg save or SAM hive copy by any attacker tool.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntds.dit access, vssadmin/diskshadow/ntdsutil execution, or NTDS file creation in any dataset.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: No SECURITY\Policy\Secrets access, lsadump, or SECURITY hive save observed.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes were by lsass.exe updating its own cached credentials; no extraction by a tool.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No drsuapi/DCSync command lines or lsadump script blocks found.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only packet-capture activity is the legitimate Azure Network Watcher agent on scranton.dmevals.local (NetworkWatcherAgent.exe -> netsh trace start capture=yes / logman ETW sessions, all parented by Azure guest-agent components). No sniffing tools, capture drivers (Npcap/WinPcap), pcap files, promiscuous-mode commands, or ICMP conn records were observed. The real attacker activity in the window (PsExec with plaintext creds launching python.exe on nashua, which beacons to 192.168.0.4:8443) is lateral movement/C2, not network sniffing.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: Obfuscated PowerShell (reflective GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle loader + base64 shellcode) executed by pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local, consistent with in-memory credential capture tooling.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: Get-Keystrokes keylogger function executed by pbeesly on scranton.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: No GUI input capture or credential-prompt abuse; the 4688 Credential/prompt check returned zero hits.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No web-root file writes, IIS/w3wp activity, or login/portal HTTP requests; related checks returned zero hits.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: Invoke-ScreenCapture screenshot-capture job executed by pbeesly on scranton.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625 failed-logon events in windows.security (count=0) and no lockout/failure messages in windows.other; no repeated authentication attempts of any kind.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No failed logons and no password-iteration loops; PowerShell *Password* hits are hardcoded-password key export and exfil scripts, not guessing.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: PowerShell.exe opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff on scranton (credential dumping) and pbeesly exported all machine certificates to .pfx with hardcoded password 'saribas'; no offline cracking tooling seen.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No 4625 failures or lockouts; the 4648 explicit-credential logons are single-account PSEXESVC lateral movement, not a one-password-many-accounts spray.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No failed logons and no many-credential-pair attempts; only single-account pbeesly reuse via PSEXESVC and hardcoded script credentials.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA/smart-card/OTP/token-interception artifacts in any dataset. Logons are ordinary Negotiate/Kerberos types; LSASS access is benign svchost.exe 0x1000; 'Credential' registry hits are CredentialGuard/CredentialEnrollmentManager OS setup. The credential-access activity present (certificate private-key export, keystroke/clipboard capture, LSASS full-access by PowerShell on scranton) is credential theft, not MFA interception.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: Zeek HTTP logs show 36 WebDAV Mini-Redirector (Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362) OPTIONS/PROPFIND requests from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4:80 returning 401 Unauthorized, the canonical forced-authentication pattern for coercing NTLM/Kerberos credentials to an attacker-controlled listener; corroborated by SMB/445 traffic to the same 192.168.0.4 host.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local a hidden, steganography-decoding PowerShell process (PID 2976, user DMEVALS\pbeesly, launched from control.exe with -ep bypass -window hidden) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 03:05:16, consistent with reading credential material from LSASS memory. Legitimate lsass access in this dataset is svchost.exe with 0x1000; the only other full-access opens are OS boot-time wininit/csrss accesses. Corroborated by remote-execution (Invoke-Command to NASHUA, Invoke-SeaDukeStage) and exfiltration staging (Invoke-Exfil) under the same user.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: All cookie-related hits are benign Windows WebDAV client operations (rundll32 davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie and the LocalService INetCookies store) and normal Edge browser file activity. No browser session cookie database was accessed by any non-browser process, no cookie-stealer tooling or cookie-referencing scripts were found (C158/C159 zero hits). The environment contains other attacker activity (PsExec with plaintext creds, python, sdelete wiping a victim file) but nothing matching T1539.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Multiple unsecured-credential artifacts: passwordsDB, hardcoded passwords in scripts, password-protected archives.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: pspasswd downloaded, accesschk created 'passwordsDB', Invoke-Exfil and Rar used hardcoded credentials/passwords; explicit-credential 4648 logons via PSEXESVC.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: All Password/Credential registry writes were by svchost/lsass/services/winlogon system processes; no adversary registry credential storage.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No consolehost_history or shell-history access found in sysmon or security datasets.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Get-PrivateKeys exported all LocalMachine certs with private keys to .pfx files using hardcoded password 'saribas' on scranton; .pfx file created by powershell.exe.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: SYSVOL/GptTmpl.inf/Groups.xml access was routine Group Policy processing by machine accounts (NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, NASHUA$); no attacker read of GPP cpassword.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: User pbeesly's powershell.exe (scranton, 03:05:16) and wsmprovhost.exe (nashua, 03:09:29) opened lsass.exe with 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff masks including read-process-memory — credential-dumping access pattern, part of a broader pbeesly intrusion.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: No browser credential files (Login Data/logins.json/cookies), browser processes as LSASS targets, or browser-credential strings in any dataset.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: LSASS full-access handle requests are the Credential Manager/DPAPI harvest mechanism, but no vault/DPAPI/Credential Manager object access or cmdkey/vaultcmd execution was observed; only benign CollectGuestLogs/MsMpEng lsass access and a benign Credential Guard config event.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: No KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden/LastPass executables, .kdbx files, or password-manager strings in any dataset.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: wsmprovhost.exe (PowerShell Remoting, user pbeesly) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff on nashua.dmevals.local, reached via PsExec with plaintext credentials from scranton; an Invoke-Exfil script with hardcoded credentials also ran on scranton. Attacker-driven access to the authentication process.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: No domain-controller authentication modification observed. The 4624 LogonType 3 events are machine-account (NEWYORK$) network logons and the 4648 explicit-credential logons are PsExec/winlogon activity; no DC authentication backdoor or Skeleton Key evidence was found.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No password filter DLL activity: no Notification Packages registry value was written and no lsass image-load of a non-Microsoft filter DLL was seen (only signed cryptdll/samlib/samcli loads).

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No reversible-encryption activity: no 4739/5136/4738 events, no Set-ADUser/dsmod/AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption command lines, and no matching PowerShell script blocks.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No MFA modification observed: no 4739/5136/4738 directory-service change events and no Set-ADUser/Set-ADAuthenticationPolicy command lines in sysmon or PowerShell.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No hybrid-identity modification observed: no 5136 directory-service change events and no Connect-MsolService/Connect-AzureAD/New-AzureAD* script blocks in PowerShell.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No network provider DLL activity: no 4657 registry change to a NetworkProvider/Credential key and no New-Item/NetworkProvider PowerShell script blocks.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: No AiTM positioning observed; the credential-related activity is plaintext-credential PsExec lateral movement (scranton->NASHUA), which is not T1557.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: DNS/WPAD lookups are routine and unanswered (NXDOMAIN); no LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning tooling and no anomalous SMB relay destination.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: Duplicate source MACs belong to separate connections and the responder MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is a placeholder; no ARP-poisoning tooling or network-config tampering.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP event codes, no DHCP PowerShell references, no zeek dhcp log type and no DHCP ports 67/68 in Sysmon connections.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: No Kerberos ticket theft or forging. 4769 tickets are normal KDC-issued AES256 tickets; 4768 AS-REQs all require pre-auth; elevated LSASS accesses are from legitimate system processes (wininit, csrss, svchost) and PowerShell/wsmprovhost whose surrounding activity is exfiltration, not ticket manipulation.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: No RC4 downgrade (all 4769 tickets are 0x12/AES256) and no anomalous krbtgt service tickets; krbtgt requests use normal TGT-renewal options 0x60810010. No golden-ticket tooling in PowerShell.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: All service tickets are KDC-issued with standard options; no evidence of tickets used without KDC validation and no silver-ticket tooling.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: No RC4 TGS requests for SPNs and no Kerberoast/Invoke-Kerberoast/Rubeus content in PowerShell script blocks.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: All 4768 AS-REQs carry PreAuthType=2 (pre-auth required); no accounts without pre-auth and no AS-REP roasting tooling observed.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No forged web credential artifacts. Logon process names are all standard; the only cookie-related process activity is benign WebDAV DavSetCookie from the exfil script's New-PSDrive, and the 'token' PowerShell hit is a Sysinternals token-attribute helper.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: No browser cookie theft/tampering or forged session cookies. Only a benign WebDAV DavSetCookie (rundll32 davclnt.dll) and a normal svchost INetCookies file write were seen.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: Zero hits for SAML/ADFS/Assertion/NotOnOrAfter in PowerShell, sysmon command lines, or zeek HTTP URLs. Kerberos traffic is normal AS/TGS for pbeesly.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No multi-factor authentication request generation activity was found. The only T1621 check with hits (windows.other 5857/5858) is benign WMI RSOP/Group Policy provider activity by SYSTEM. windows.security has zero 4625 failed logons, no MFA/2FA/authenticator strings appear in PowerShell 4104 script blocks, and sysmon 'push' matches are built-in Windows services (PushToInstall, dmwappushservice).

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: Certificate private-key export to .pfx via Get-PrivateKeys on scranton (new artifact beyond the anchor).

checks.purpose: Stack all process creations to spot credential-dumping tools (mimikatz, procdump, comsvcs.dll rundll32) among rare executables.
Stack process-access targets to find LSASS or other credential-store processes being opened.
Stack object types accessed under handle/object-access auditing to find SAM/SECURITY/LSASS objects.
Stack newly created processes to spot dumping utilities launched on hosts.

args.query: event.code:4104 AND (powershell.script_block_text:*lsass* OR powershell.script_block_text:*mimikatz* OR powershell.script_block_text:*sekurlsa* OR powershell.script_block_text:*DumpCreds*)

checks.purpose: Find PowerShell script blocks referencing LSASS/credential-dumping APIs.
Look for credential-dumping references in other Windows event channels (service installs, VSS, etc.).
Stack granted-access masks on LSASS process opens to reveal memory-read access typical of dumping.
Read individual LSASS access events with source image and granted access.

function Invoke-Discovery {
    $DiscoveryInfo =@()
    $CurrentDir = Get-Location

    $DiscoveryInfo += [PSCustomObject]@{
                CurrentDirectory = $CurrentDir
                TempDirectory = $env:TEMP
                UserName = $env:USERNAME
                ComputerName = $env:COMPUTERNAME
                UserDomain = $env:USERDOMAIN

args.query: FROM logs-windows.powershell-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code IN ("4103","4104") AND (TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*login data*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*logins.json*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*key3.db*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*key4.db*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*sharpchrome*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*lazagne*") | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, powershell.script_block_text, _id, _index

checks.purpose: PowerShell scripts targeting browser credential stores or running browser-credential extraction modules.

args.query: FROM logs-windows.other-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE TO_LOWER(COALESCE(message, win.Message, "")) LIKE "*login data*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(message, win.Message, "")) LIKE "*logins.json*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(message, win.Message, "")) LIKE "*chrome*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(message, win.Message, "")) LIKE "*firefox*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, event.code, message, _id, _index

checks.purpose: Other Windows channels may log browser credential-store file access or browser-related activity.
Detect processes opening handles to lsass.exe, which is how Credential Manager secrets (DPAPI vaults) are commonly harvested.

findings.title: LSASS memory accessed with full-access masks by PowerShell and PowerShell Remoting host under user pbeesly
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02, user pbeesly obtained handles to lsass.exe with full-access masks from PowerShell processes on two hosts. On scranton.dmevals.local, powershell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF at 03:05:16; the same access was recorded in Windows Security 4656 with AccessMask 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff. On nashua.dmevals.local, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, PowerShell Remoting) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29, also seen in Security 4656 with AccessMask 0x1f3fff. The call traces run through PowerShell/System.Management.Automation native images, consistent with in-memory LSASS credential dumping. This occurred in the middle of a pbeesly PowerShell toolkit session (Get-PrivateKeys, Get-Keystrokes, Invoke-ScreenCapture, Invoke-Exfil) on scranton.

findings.title: Obfuscated PowerShell with reflective code loading and base64 shellcode on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed a PowerShell script block (EventID 4104, ScriptBlockId bc19aae2-d1f9-49b2-b718-192531ae928f) that defines functions using Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle and DefineDynamicAssembly/DefineDynamicModule to build an in-memory delegate, then decodes a base64 byte array ([System.Convert]::FromBase64String) — a reflective shellcode loader. A child process was spawned as powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -e <base64> whose parent command line was powershell.exe -c "Get-ItemPropertyValue 'HKLM:\\SOFTWARE\Javasoft' 'value Supplement' | Invoke-Expression", i.e. hidden encoded execution. This tooling is consistent with in-memory credential capture on the host.

findings.title: PowerShell opens LSASS with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS (0x1FFFFF) using reflective/injected code
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 2020-05-02T03:05:16.654Z. The CallTrace shows only ntdll.dll/KERNELBASE.dll followed by UNKNOWN(000001996D28200D), indicating the calling code is not backed by a known module (reflectively loaded/injected code) — the classic signature of credential API hooking / in-memory credential theft. A second open with 0x1f3fff occurred at 03:05:16.623Z. This is the same host/user (pbeesly) that ran an obfuscated PowerShell script using GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle and a base64 shellcode blob.

On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed Invoke-ScreenCapture at 03:05:53, a background job that repeatedly captures the screen to random-named .bmp files in $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads. Screen capture can harvest credentials displayed on screen.

findings.title: PowerShell script exported all LocalMachine certificates with private keys to .pfx files on scranton.dmevals.local
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:04:56 UTC on host scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed a PowerShell script block named 'Get-PrivateKeys' (ScriptBlock ID 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1). The script recursively enumerates cert:\LocalMachine, and for every certificate with a Thumbprint exports it with Export-PfxCertificate to a randomly named .pfx file under $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads, protected by the hardcoded password 'saribas'. This is direct theft of authentication certificates and their private keys (T1649). The export is corroborated by Sysmon: powershell.exe read HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\MY\Certificates\48B5E43D09D080DF8863152FD22ED7C43443D499\Blob and ...\Remote Desktop\Certificates\615B93C2D2B647D1670500B3338EAAEC83BA5646\Blob at 03:04:57, and wrote C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx at 03:04:57.460. The activity is preceded (02:58:44) by a hidden, execution-policy-bypassed PowerShell launched by control.exe that decodes a payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png and IEXes it, indicating an initial stager on the same host/user. The certificate registry writes on other hosts (svchost.exe/lsass.exe/taskhostw.exe touching AuthRoot, Windows Live ID Token Issuer, ACRS stores) are normal OS certificate-store maintenance and are not attributed to the attacker.

findings.title: Attacker activity in window is PsExec lateral movement and python C2, not network sniffing
findings.summary: The genuine malicious activity in this window is unrelated to T1040: on scranton.dmevals.local, PsExec64.exe (parent powershell.exe, user pbeesly) repeatedly runs against \\NASHUA with plaintext credentials (-u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by) to launch C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe. On nashua.dmevals.local that python.exe (parent C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe, user pbeesly) then opens hundreds of TCP connections to 192.168.0.4:8443. This is lateral movement/execution and C2, not credential sniffing, so it does not satisfy T1040; it is noted here only to distinguish it from the benign capture activity.

Zeek conn records show outbound SMB traffic to 192.168.0.4: 10 connections on port 445 (all from 10.0.1.4) and 5 on port 139, alongside 392 total connections from 10.0.1.6 (376) and 10.0.1.4 (16) to 192.168.0.4. Sysmon event code 3 confirms a connection from nashua.dmevals.local to 10.0.0.4:445. The same 192.168.0.4 host is the WebDAV coercion target, so the SMB traffic to it is consistent with the same forced-authentication/credential-capture activity rather than ordinary file sharing.

LSASS handle requests by user processes (Credential Manager/DPAPI harvest mechanism) — no vault object access observed
findings.summary: The LSASS handle requests with 0x1fffff (scranton, powershell.exe, pbeesly) and 0x1f3fff (nashua, wsmprovhost.exe, pbeesly) are the mechanism by which Windows Credential Manager / DPAPI secrets held in LSASS memory would be harvested, so they are relevant to T1555.004. However, no direct access to Credential Manager vault objects, DPAPI Protect/Credential/Vault object names, or cmdkey/vaultcmd execution was observed: the only credential-related object-access events on lsass.exe were from C:\WindowsAzure\Packages\CollectGuestLogs.exe (Azure guest log collection, benign) and Windows Defender MsMpEng.exe, and the only 'Credential' string in windows.other was the benign 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0' event on scranton. The credential-store-specific artifact is therefore not directly observed; the LSASS access is attributed to T1555 broadly.

findings.title: Azure Network Watcher packet capture on scranton.dmevals.local is legitimate platform monitoring, not adversary sniffing
findings.summary: The only packet-capture activity in the dataset is the Azure Network Watcher agent on scranton.dmevals.local. NetworkWatcherAgent.exe (parent C:\Windows\System32\services.exe, user SYSTEM) starts a capture via netsh.exe 'trace start capture=yes traceFile=...etl' and manages ETW trace sessions with logman.exe (GAEvents/RTEvents, output to C:\WindowsAzure\Logs\*.etl). All parent processes are Azure guest-agent components (WaAppAgent.exe, WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe, services.exe) and the binaries live under C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher... and C:\WindowsAzure\Packages. This is the standard Azure VM network-capture/diagnostics agent, not an adversary sniffing tool. No tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap, no Npcap/WinPcap driver load, no pcap files, and no promiscuous-mode commands were observed on any host.

findings.title: No sniffing tooling, capture drivers or pcap artifacts found on any host

The only .etl files created are OS/Azure diagnostic logs (ProvTool, waasmedic, SleepStudy, WDI, DiagnosticLogCSP) written by System/svchost/ProvTool. findings.summary: Hunting for T1111 (Multi-Factor Authentication Interception) across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and windows.other produced no evidence of MFA interception. All 297 successful logons (4624) are ordinary types (3 network=218, 5 service=61, 2 interactive=15, 10 RDP=2, 0=1) using Negotiate/Kerberos; the 218 Kerberos logons are machine-account (computer$) network logons on newyork.dmevals.local. The 15 explicit-credential logons (4648) are pbeesly via PSEXESVC.exe/svchost.exe and built-in DWM/UMFD/winlogon accounts. LSASS access (Sysmon 10, 326 events) is dominated by svchost.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION) — normal. Registry 'Credential' hits are CredentialGuard/CredentialEnrollmentManager service setup by lsass.exe/services.exe — benign OS activity. No smart-card, OTP, token-interception, or credential-provider tampering was observed. However, the same window contains genuine credential-access activity on scranton.dmevals.local by user pbeesly (a PowerShell toolkit psversion.ps1/readme.ps1 exporting machine certificate private keys, capturing keystrokes/clipboard/screenshots, and PowerShell.exe opening LSASS with full access 0x1FFFFF) — this is credential theft (T1552.004/T1056.001/T1003), not MFA interception, so it is reported here as context rather than as a T1111 hit.

Security events 5140/5145 on newyork.dmevals.local show network share access to \\*\SYSVOL from machine accounts NEWYORK$ (fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429) and SCRANTON$ (10.0.1.4). These are domain-controller SYSVOL/Group Policy reads by computer accounts, a routine AD replication/GPO pattern, not credential coercion. No attacker-controlled listener or credential capture is evidenced here.
findings.title: Inbound SMB share access to SYSVOL on newyork from SCRANTON$ and NEWYORK$ machine accounts

findings.summary: The 42 Kerberos events (28x 4769, 14x 4768) on newyork.dmevals.local are ordinary service-ticket requests by the domain account pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL and machine accounts (SCRANTON$) from client addresses 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6, requesting tickets for NEWYORK$, NASHUA$ and krbtgt. No anomalous encryption downgrade, no RC4-only pattern, no ticket-forging indicators were observed; these are normal domain logon/ticket-granting activity and do not by themselves evidence exploitation for credential access.
findings.title: Kerberos service-ticket requests (4768/4769) are routine domain authentication, not exploitation

findings.title: WebDAV client cookie operations (DavSetCookie / INetCookies) on scranton — benign
findings.summary: The only 'cookie'-matching process activity is the Windows WebDAV client: rundll32.exe loading davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie to set a WebDAV cookie for the mount http://192.168.0.4/webdav, run as user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local (5 events, 2020-05-02 03:08:50–03:10:23). The matching Sysmon file-creation is svchost.exe creating the LocalService INetCookies store under a Windows package AC directory. These are standard WebDAV/IE cookie-store operations, not theft of browser session cookies.

findings.title: Edge browser file activity on scranton/nashua — benign browser operation
findings.summary: Sysmon file-creation and process-access events touching MicrosoftEdge.exe/MicrosoftEdgeCP.exe are generated by the browser itself (Temp, Recovery, DataStore files) and by Explorer.exe (GrantedAccess 0x2000) and svchost.exe (0x3000) on nashua.dmevals.local. No non-browser process read or copied a browser cookie database (no Cookies/Login Data/Web Data file access was found).

findings.title: No web session cookie theft observed; environment shows unrelated attacker activity
findings.summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and windows.other there is no evidence of browser session cookie theft: no cookie-stealer tooling, no access to browser cookie stores, and no cookie-referencing PowerShell script blocks (C158/C159 zero hits). The environment does contain other attacker activity (PsExec64.exe with plaintext credentials to \\NASHUA, python.exe, sdelete64.exe wiping C:\programdata\victim\???cod.3aka3.scr), but none of it constitutes T1539.

findings.title: Registry Password/Credential value writes are OS service activity
findings.summary: The 17 Sysmon event-13 registry writes matching Password/Credential keys on nashua/scranton are all performed by legitimate system processes: svchost.exe writing HKU\.DEFAULT\Software\Microsoft\IdentityCRL\ProviderPasswordLength/CharacterGroups, lsass.exe writing DeviceGuard\Scenarios\CredentialGuard\Enabled, services.exe writing CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service keys, and winlogon.exe writing Winlogon\PasswordExpiryNotification. None represent an adversary storing or harvesting credentials in the registry.

findings.title: SYSVOL GPO file access is normal machine-account Group Policy processing
findings.summary: SMB/SYSVOL access to GPO files (gpt.ini, GptTmpl.inf, SecEdit, Machine\Microsoft\Windows NT) was observed in both zeek (2020-04-30, observers simplerockbuild.simplerock.lan and bobs.bigwheel.local reading \\NEWYORK.dmevals.local\sysvol) and windows.security 5145 events on newyork.dmevals.local. All 5145 subjects are machine accounts (NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, NASHUA$) performing routine Group Policy refresh, and the zeek smb_files records are SMB::FILE_OPEN of standard policy paths. No Groups.xml with cpassword was read by a user account, and no attacker process accessed SYSVOL. This is expected domain behaviour, not GPP credential harvesting.

findings.title: No browser credential-store access observed
findings.summary: No evidence of web-browser credential theft was found. Searches for browser credential artifacts (Login Data, logins.json, cookies) in Sysmon file-create events, for browser processes (chrome.exe/firefox.exe) as LSASS access targets, and for browser-credential strings in PowerShell script blocks and Windows security object-access events returned no hits. The only cookie-related file event was an INetCookies file under a LocalService package profile on scranton, which is normal OS/app behaviour.

findings.title: Routine LSASS handle access by svchost and security agents (benign baseline)
findings.summary: The bulk of the 326 LSASS-access events are benign: 289 from C:\windows\system32\svchost.exe and 28 from Microsoft Azure security/telemetry agents (AntimalwareConfig.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe), overwhelmingly with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION) or 0x1400. These are normal Windows service and AV/telemetry reads of LSASS, not authentication-process modification. The two powershell.exe LSASS accesses on scranton (0x1000, call trace through System.ni.dll) are likewise low-privilege query access.

findings.title: Benign cryptdll/samlib/samcli image loads into normal Windows processes
findings.summary: The 77 image-load hits for lsass/cryptdll/sam/msv1_0 are ordinary Microsoft-signed DLL loads (cryptdll.dll 'Cryptography Manager', samlib.dll 'SAM Library DLL', samcli.dll 'Security Accounts Manager Client DLL') into legitimate processes such as SearchProtocolHost.exe, SearchFilterHost.exe, WmiPrvSE.exe, svchost.exe, dsregcmd.exe and powershell.exe. No unsigned or non-Microsoft module was loaded into LSASS, so this does not indicate authentication-process modification.

findings.title: Benign LSA registry writes by lsass.exe and password-expiry notifications
findings.summary: Registry writes touching LSA/password keys are normal OS behaviour: lsass.exe writing HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\ProductType, LsaCfgFlagsDefault and LsaPid on scranton, svchost.exe writing IdentityCRL ProviderPasswordLength/CharacterGroups, and winlogon.exe writing the per-user PasswordExpiryNotification NotShownReason. No Notification Packages (password filter DLL) or NetworkProvider value was modified, so no T1556.002/T1556.008 persistence was established.

findings.title: No adversary-in-the-middle activity; observed credential theft is PsExec-based lateral movement, not AiTM
findings.summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.other, windows.powershell and zeek there is no evidence of an adversary positioned in the middle of network traffic. The only credential-related activity is plaintext-credential lateral movement: on scranton.dmevals.local user pbeesly ran PsExec64.exe against \\NASHUA with explicit credentials (-u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by) to launch C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe, which installed the PSEXESVC service on nashua.dmevals.local. That is T1021.002/T1078/T1003 territory, not T1557. Object-access stacking (4663/4670/4656) shows only routine processes (powershell, svchost, WmiPrvSE, services, lsass) touching Key/Token/File objects, and Sysmon network connections (event 3) show normal domain traffic (LDAP 389, Kerberos 88, SMB 445, DNS 53) with no unexpected relay host.

findings.title: No name-resolution poisoning or SMB relay; DNS/WPAD lookups are routine and unanswered
findings.summary: Name-resolution activity is normal. Zeek DNS shows wpad.dmevals.local queried by 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6 returning NXDOMAIN (routine WPAD auto-discovery with no rogue WPAD responder answering), plus ordinary single-label NetBIOS-style lookups for SCRANTON/NASHUA and LDAP SRV records. Sysmon event 22 query names are all legitimate (host names, microsoft.com/azureedge telemetry, ocsp.digicert.com). No LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning tooling appears in PowerShell script blocks, and no SMB relay destination stands out: SMB (445) connections are between domain hosts (e.g. 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.5/10.0.1.6 to 10.0.0.4) with normal machine-account logons (NASHUA$, NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, WEC$).

findings.title: No ARP cache poisoning; duplicate MACs are separate connections / lab placeholder
findings.summary: Zeek conn records show host 10.0.1.4 reaching 10.0.1.6 with two different source MACs (00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 and fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) and a responder MAC of 12:34:56:78:9a:bc. These are distinct connections at distinct timestamps, not one MAC claiming multiple IPs simultaneously, and 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is a synthetic/placeholder address rather than a real gratuitous-ARP spoof. No ARP-poisoning tooling (arp/netsh interface) appears in PowerShell script blocks, and no network-configuration object tampering is visible in the 4663/4670/4656 object-access events.

findings.title: No Kerberos ticket theft or forging observed; LSASS accesses are legitimate system processes
findings.summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon and zeek there is no evidence of Kerberos ticket theft or forging. The 4769 service-ticket requests on newyork.dmevals.local are normal KDC-issued tickets (AES256, TicketOptions 0x40810000/0x60810010 = forwardable/renewable TGT renewal), and the 4768 AS-REQs all carry PreAuthType=2 (pre-authentication required). LSASS handle accesses with elevated masks (0x1fffff, 0x1f3fff, 0x101001) come from legitimate Windows components (wininit.exe, csrss.exe, svchost.exe) and from PowerShell/wsmprovhost whose surrounding activity is exfiltration, not ticket manipulation. No ticket-forging or roasting tooling was found.

findings.title: No golden-ticket indicators: no RC4 downgrade and no anomalous krbtgt service tickets
findings.summary: All 28 Kerberos service-ticket requests (event 4769) on newyork.dmevals.local use TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256), with no RC4 (0x17/0x18) downgrade that would suggest a forged golden ticket. The three krbtgt service-ticket requests (by pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL and SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL) carry TicketOptions 0x60810010, consistent with legitimate TGT renewal rather than forged-ticket use. No golden-ticket forging tooling was found in PowerShell script blocks.

findings.title: No silver-ticket indicators: all service tickets are KDC-issued with normal options
findings.summary: The 4769 service-ticket requests on newyork.dmevals.local target machine accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) and krbtgt, all with TicketEncryptionType 0x12 and standard TicketOptions (0x40800000/0x40810000/0x60810010). There is no evidence of service tickets being used without corresponding KDC validation, and no silver-ticket tooling in PowerShell script blocks.

findings.title: No Kerberoasting: no RC4 TGS requests for SPNs and no roasting tooling
findings.summary: No Kerberos service-ticket requests used RC4 encryption (all 4769 events are 0x12/AES256), which is the hallmark of Kerberoasting. The PowerShell script blocks contain no Kerberoast/Invoke-Kerberoast/Rubeus content. The only notable PowerShell activity on scranton.dmevals.local by user pbeesly is an exfiltration script (Invoke-Exfil compressing Downloads and copying to a WebDAV share), which is unrelated to Kerberoasting.

The PowerShell 4104 search for SAML/NotOnOrAfter/Assertion returned zero hits; the sysmon process search for saml/token/cert command lines returned zero hits; the zeek HTTP search for saml/adfs/token URLs returned zero hits. Kerberos traffic in the zeek window is normal AS/TGS exchange for pbeesly (krbtgt/DMEVALS.LOCAL, cifs/NASHUA, HTTP/NASHUA, ldap/NEWYORK) with standard KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED, and logon process names are all standard. No federated-identity or token-signing material was touched.

WMI RSOP/Group Policy activity in windows.other is benign, not MFA request generation
findings.summary: The only hit for the T1621 hypothesis was 85 WMI-Activity events (event.code 5857/5858) in windows.other on newyork.dmevals.local. Full-event inspection shows these are standard WMI provider starts (dsccore, CIMWin32, deploymentprovider, dnsclientcim, StorageWMI) and RSOP_ExtensionStatus DeleteInstance operations under Root\Rsop\Computer, executed by NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (S-1-5-18) via wmiprvse.exe. This is routine Group Policy/RSOP processing, not multi-factor authentication request generation. No MFA/2FA/authenticator/push-notification activity was found in any dataset.

findings.title: No failed-logon or MFA-fatigue pattern in windows.security
findings.summary: windows.security contains zero event.code 4625 (failed logon) events, so there is no repeated authentication-failure pattern that would accompany an MFA fatigue / request-generation campaign. The only authentication-related events are explicit-credential logons (4648) and NTLM validation (4776) for user pbeesly across scranton/nashua/newyork, which are normal interactive/remote logon activity.

findings.title: Sysmon 'push' matches are Windows services, not MFA push notifications
findings.summary: A sysmon process-creation search for mfa/authenticator/2fa/push returned only three benign Windows service processes on scranton.dmevals.local: svchost.exe hosting PushToInstall, sc.exe starting 'pushtoinstall registration', and svchost.exe hosting dmwappushservice. These are built-in Windows services and unrelated to multi-factor authentication request generation.

findings.title: Kerberos TGT requests and certificate-store registry writes on other hosts show no certificate-forging activity
findings.summary: The remaining T1649 check hits are consistent with normal Windows behaviour. Kerberos AS-REQ (event 4768) activity in windows.security is limited to the account pbeesly (9 requests) and the machine account SCRANTON$ (5 requests), all with Status 0x0 from internal addresses 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6 on newyork.dmevals.local — ordinary domain logon traffic, not certificate-based authentication abuse. The certificate/crypto registry writes in windows.sysmon are dominated by OS components (svchost.exe, lsass.exe, taskhostw.exe, smss.exe) touching AuthRoot, Windows Live ID Token Issuer, ACRS PhysicalStores and SymbolicLinkValue keys, i.e. routine certificate-store maintenance. The Zeek x509 subjects (rempel.group.net, conn.sons.info) are external TLS server certificates from a non-overlapping window and show no forged authentication certificates. None of these constitute attacker certificate theft or forging.

findings.title: No DHCP spoofing; no DHCP-related telemetry present
findings.summary: No DHCP spoofing indicators exist in the data. The windows.other System channel contains no DHCP-related event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063 absent from the code distribution), no PowerShell script block references DHCP, and the zeek capture contains no dhcp log type (only conn/files/ssl/x509/dce_rpc/http/dns/kerberos/dpd/smb_files/smb_mapping/weird/notice/pe). Sysmon network connections show no DHCP ports 67/68. The technique is therefore not observable in this dataset rather than positively benign.

incidents.title: PowerShell credential-collection toolkit (Get-PrivateKeys, Get-Keystrokes, Invoke-ScreenCapture, Invoke-Exfil) on scranton
incidents.rationale: Single finding covering the psversion.ps1 toolkit run by pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local; the credential-collection script blocks are best captured as OS Credential Dumping.

incidents.title: LSASS memory accessed with full-access masks by PowerShell and WinRM host under pbeesly
incidents.rationale: All four findings describe the same action: handles to lsass.exe opened with full-access masks (0x1F3FFF / 0x1FFFFF) by powershell.exe on scranton.dmevals.local and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua.dmevals.local under user pbeesly, sharing the same lsass handle events. This is OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory.

incidents.title: Credential material accessed via LSASS handle and private-key export (not offline cracking)
incidents.rationale: The finding describes LSASS handle access with full-access masks on scranton.dmevals.local, i.e. in-memory credential dumping rather than password cracking; best fit is LSASS Memory.

incidents.title: Get-Keystrokes keylogger function executed on scranton
incidents.rationale: Execution of the Get-Keystrokes keylogger on scranton.dmevals.local is input capture via keylogging.

incidents.title: Invoke-ScreenCapture screenshot capture function executed on scranton
incidents.rationale: Invoke-ScreenCapture repeatedly captures the screen to harvest displayed credentials, matching credential API hooking/input capture.

incidents.title: WebDAV Mini-Redirector forced authentication from scranton to 192.168.0.4
incidents.rationale: WebDAV Mini-Redirector requests from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4 receiving 401 is the classic forced-authentication pattern.

incidents.title: SMB/445 connections to 192.168.0.4 from scranton and nashua workstations
incidents.rationale: SMB traffic to the same 192.168.0.4 host used as the WebDAV coercion target is consistent with the same forced-authentication/credential-capture activity.

incidents.title: Steganographic PowerShell payload opens LSASS with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS on scranton
incidents.rationale: The finding attributes the steganographic payload and subsequent LSASS full-access open to exploitation for credential access.

incidents.title: accesschk.exe run by pbeesly creates a file named 'passwordsDB' on scranton
incidents.rationale: A file named for a password database produced by accesschk.exe under pbeesly is unsecured-credentials collection.

incidents.title: Plaintext credentials in files/command lines: passwordsDB artifact and PsExec -p password
incidents.rationale: Cleartext credentials handled by pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local, including the passwordsDB file and the plaintext -p password on the PsExec command line.

incidents.title: Invoke-Exfil PowerShell script with hardcoded credentials on SCRANTON
incidents.rationale: Hardcoded credentials ($UserName 'cozy', $Password 'MyCozyPassw0rd!') embedded in the Invoke-Exfil script are credentials in files.

incidents.title: pspasswd.exe downloaded and accesschk.exe used to create 'passwordsDB' file on scranton
incidents.rationale: Credential material staged to disk via the 'passwordsDB' artifact created by accesschk.exe, with pspasswd staged alongside.

incidents.title: Invoke-Exfil with hardcoded credentials and archive password on scranton
incidents.rationale: Plaintext credentials ('cozy'/'MyCozyPassw0rd!') and archive password 'lolol' embedded in the Invoke-Exfil script are credentials in files.

incidents.title: Password-protected Rar archive of user profile created on nashua with hardcoded password
incidents.rationale: Rar.exe created a password-protected archive of collected credential-related files using the hardcoded password 'fGzq5yKw'.

incidents.title: Explicit-credential logons (4648) with pbeesly from scranton to nashua via PSEXESVC
incidents.rationale: Explicit-credential logon events showing pbeesly authenticating via PSEXESVC reflect credential use consistent with the plaintext-credential PsExec activity.

incidents.title: Get-PrivateKeys exports LocalMachine certificates with private keys using hardcoded password 'saribas' on scranton
incidents.rationale: Private keys exported from the certificate store to .pfx files constitute private-key theft.

incidents.title: LSASS handle requests by user processes (Credential Manager/DPAPI harvest mechanism)
incidents.rationale: The finding frames the LSASS handle requests as the mechanism for harvesting Windows Credential Manager/DPAPI secrets, with no vault object access observed.

incidents.title: PowerShell script exported all LocalMachine certificates with private keys to .pfx files on scranton
incidents.rationale: Get-PrivateKeys exported every LocalMachine certificate with private keys to .pfx files, i.e. stealing authentication certificates.

incidents.title: PsExec lateral movement to NASHUA with python C2 (not network sniffing)
incidents.rationale: The finding itself states the activity is PsExec lateral movement and python C2, not T1040 network sniffing; remote services execution is out of scope for credential access.

incidents.title: PsExec with plaintext credentials used to move to NASHUA and install PSEXESVC
incidents.rationale: PsExec with credentials to install PSEXESVC and execute on NASHUA is remote services lateral movement, not credential access.

incidents.title: Obfuscated PowerShell with reflective code loading and base64 shellcode on scranton
incidents.rationale: Reflective shellcode loader and hidden base64 PowerShell execution is execution/defense evasion, not credential access.

FROM logs-windows.powershell-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "4104" | WHERE TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*pspasswd*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*passwordsdb*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*pfx*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*privatekey*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*export*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*rar.exe*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*sdelete*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, message, _id, _index | SORT @timestamp ASC

FROM logs-windows.powershell-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "4104" | WHERE TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*pspasswd*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*passwordsdb*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*export-pfxcertificate*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*rar.exe*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*sdelete*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*working.zip*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, message, _id, _index | SORT @timestamp ASC

FROM logs-windows.security-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "4688" | WHERE TO_LOWER(process.command_line) LIKE "*pspasswd*" OR TO_LOWER(process.command_line) LIKE "*passwordsdb*" OR TO_LOWER(process.command_line) LIKE "*pfx*" OR TO_LOWER(process.command_line) LIKE "*rar.exe*" OR TO_LOWER(process.command_line) LIKE "*sdelete*" OR TO_LOWER(process.command_line) LIKE "*accesschk*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, process.executable, process.command_line, process.parent.executable, _id, _index | SORT @timestamp ASC

FROM logs-windows.powershell-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "4104" | WHERE TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*get-keystrokes*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*get-privatekeys*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*invoke-screencapture*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*invoke-exfil*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*pspasswd*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*mimikatz*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*sekurlsa*" OR TO_LOWER(message) LIKE "*lsass*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, message, _id, _index | SORT @timestamp ASC

FROM logs-windows.sysmon-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "1" | WHERE TO_LOWER(process.command_line) LIKE "*pspasswd*" OR TO_LOWER(process.executable) LIKE "*pspasswd*" OR TO_LOWER(process.command_line) LIKE "*accesschk*" OR TO_LOWER(process.command_line) LIKE "*readme.ps1*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, process.executable, process.command_line, process.parent.executable, _id, _index | SORT @timestamp ASC

FROM logs-windows.security-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "4624" OR event.code == "4648" | WHERE TO_LOWER(winlog.event_data.TargetUserName) LIKE "*pbeesly*" OR TO_LOWER(winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName) LIKE "*pbeesly*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, winlog.event_data.TargetUserName, winlog.event_data.LogonType, winlog.event_data.IpAddress, winlog.event_data.ProcessName, _id, _index | SORT @timestamp ASC
